# External Commands

## Overview

The Entire CLI supports kubectl-style external commands — standalone binaries on `$PATH` that extend the CLI without modifying the main repository. When the user invokes `entire <name>` and `<name>` isn't a built-in subcommand, the CLI looks for an `entire-<name>` binary on `$PATH` and execs it with the remaining arguments. Stdio passes through, exit codes propagate, and the parent CLI does no further processing of the child's output.

This is not the same mechanism as the external agent protocol. External commands have no protocol, no JSON contract, no lifecycle hooks. Use the agent protocol when you need checkpoint integration; use external commands for everything else.

## Resolution

The CLI does not scan `$PATH` at startup. Resolution is lazy: when `os.Args[1]` doesn't match a built-in subcommand, the CLI calls `exec.LookPath("entire-" + os.Args[1])`. If a binary is found and executable, it runs before Cobra parses arguments.

Rules, in order:

  1. Built-ins win. If the first argument matches a Cobra subcommand (or one of its aliases), the external command is never considered.
  2. Reserved names are skipped. Names beginning with `agent-` are reserved for the agent protocol. The resolver refuses to invoke them as external commands.
  3. Path-traversal candidates are rejected. Names containing `/` or `\` never resolve.
  4. Found-but-not-executable surfaces as a launch error. If `entire-<name>` exists on `$PATH` but lacks the executable bit, the resolver reports `Failed to run plugin entire-<name>` with exit code 1, rather than falling through to Cobra's "unknown command" path.

### Managed install directory

Users can drop binaries anywhere on `$PATH`, but a per-user managed directory is also automatically discovered:

  * Default: `$XDG_DATA_HOME/entire/plugins/bin` (Linux/macOS) or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\entire\plugins\bin` (Windows).
  * Override: `$ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR/bin`.

The CLI prepends this directory to `$PATH` at startup via `cli.PrependPluginBinDirToPATH()` so the existing `exec.LookPath` resolution finds managed installs without any special-casing. This is purely additive — the kubectl-style `$PATH` model is unchanged.

`entire plugin install/list/remove` manage the contents of this directory. Authors who prefer the raw "drop a binary on `$PATH`" model don't need to use it.

> Compatibility note: the `entire plugin` command group is itself a built-in. Per the "built-ins win" rule above, it shadows any external command named `entire-plugin` that may have existed on `$PATH` previously. The collision is intentional — managing plugins is a built-in concern — but worth flagging for anyone who shipped an `entire-plugin` external command before this layer landed.

## Environment

Each external-command invocation receives:

Variable  | Description
--- | ---
`ENTIRE_CLI_VERSION`  | The CLI's version string (e.g. `0.42.0`, `dev`)
`ENTIRE_REPO_ROOT`  | Absolute path to the git repository root, when the CLI is invoked inside one. Omitted otherwise.
`ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DATA_DIR`  | Per-plugin durable storage directory (`<plugin-root>/data/<name>`). Not pre-created — the plugin should `mkdir -p` on first write. Set regardless of whether the plugin is on raw `$PATH` or in the managed dir, so plugins get the same contract either way. Omitted only in degenerate environments where the per-user data root cannot be resolved (e.g. no home dir, no `LOCALAPPDATA`/`XDG_DATA_HOME`/`ENTIRE_PLUGIN_DIR`); the parent CLI prints a warning to stderr in that case.

The working directory is not changed — external commands run in the user's current directory, the same as any other shell command.

### Environment filtering

Unlike `kubectl` and `gh`, which forward the parent's full environment to every plugin, Entire filters the parent environment through a small allowlist before invoking an external command. ## Adding an Entire-Shipped Command to the Allowlist

When publishing an Entire-owned external command (e.g. `entire-pgr`):

  1. Append the command name to `officialPlugins` in `cmd/entire/cli/plugin_official.go`.
  2. Match must be exact and case-sensitive — the binary on disk is `entire-<name>`.
  3. Update or add tests if the command has unusual telemetry shape.

Once allowlisted, `cli_plugin_executed` events for that command will flow through the existing PostHog pipeline.

## Comparison with the Agent Protocol

 | External Commands  | Agent Protocol
--- | --- | ---
Binary name pattern  | `entire-<name>`  | `entire-agent-<name>`
Discovery  | Lazy, on first non-built-in arg  | Lazy at command entry, gated by `external_agents` setting (setup flows bypass the gate via `DiscoverAndRegisterAlways`)
Communication  | Process exec; stdio passthrough  | Subcommand protocol; JSON over stdin/stdout
Versioning  | None  | `ENTIRE_PROTOCOL_VERSION` envelope
Lifecycle integration  | None  | Full (sessions, checkpoints, hooks, transcripts)

{"body":"## Summary
`entire agent add/list/remove` omitted external agents (e.g. `zed`), failing with `Unknown agent`, even though `entire enable --agent <name>` and the git-hook paths worked. The `agent` noun-group never invoked external-agent discovery, so `agent.Get` / `agent.List` only saw statically-registered built-ins.

Fixes #1928.

## Changes
- `add` / `remove` `RunE`: resolve the single named plugin via the shared `resolveNamedExternalAgent` helper (`external.DiscoverAndRegisterNamedAlways(ctx, name)`) before `agent.Get` / `runRemoveAgent`. Targeting the exact name (rather than a full `$PATH` scan) avoids executing every unrelated `entire-agent-*` binary, and surfaces a real plugin load error instead of a generic "unknown agent". Built-in names short-circuit instantly (no exec); an unknown name still falls through to `printWrongAgentError`. These bypass the `external_agents` gate because the action is itself the opt-in — and `add` auto-persists `external_agents=true` for an external agent (via `setupAgentHooksNonInteractive`).
- `entire agent list`: **default lists built-in agents only** — no `$PATH` scan and no plugin exec, so the listing stays fast regardless of how many `entire-agent-*` binaries are on `$PATH`.
  - Because that view is partial, it **says so**: the header is `Built-in agents:` (not the `--external` view's `Agents:`), and the footer reports when the repo has `external_agents` enabled but is not showing those plugins. Without this, the user who had just run `entire agent add <plugin>` — which turns the gate on — got a listing under a completeness-implying header that silently excluded the agent they had installed, and an empty state reading `No built-in agents installed.`
  - Reading the setting for that footer is one file read and no plugin exec, so the no-scan guarantee is unchanged (`TestRunAgentList_DefaultPathDoesNotScanPath` still passes untouched). The alternative — having the default path honour the gate and discover — was rejected deliberately: `entire agent list` would then change both cost and content off a setting the user never typed.
- **`--external`** is a **superset**: it lists the built-in agents *and* the external plugins on `$PATH` (installed and available) via full discovery, reusing the built-in rendering — installed `✓` marker, sort order, and test-only filter — so the two views differ only where they must (its header is unscoped, and it is the view whose empty state can honestly say `No agents installed.`). External entries carry an `(external)` suffix, because they are arbitrary executables resolved from `$PATH` rather than code shipped in the binary, and that distinction is trust-relevant.
  - This replaces the earlier `--all` flag. Previously the default path executed every plugin on `$PATH` to mark installed externals — a per-plugin exec cost that scaled with plugin count on a sub-100ms command. All external work is now behind the explicit `--external` opt-in.
- Discovery lives in the run function (not the group's `PersistentPreRunE`), so unit tests calling `runAgentList` directly exercise it.
- **`printAgentError` (the "Unknown agent" / "Missing agent name" path) no longer contradicts `agent list`**:
  - It goes through the new `agent.ListAvailable`, so test-only agents (`vogon`) are no longer advertised as available.
  - The trailing hint now follows one rule: **it exists only to cover a listing that is knowably incomplete.** What the caller did about `$PATH` before giving up on the name decides which hint, if any, is honest.
    - A full `$PATH` scan already ran, so the listing is complete → **no hint**. This is `enable --agent`, which runs `DiscoverAndRegisterAlways` at `setup.go:892` fourteen lines before the failing `agent.Get`: every plugin is already in the listing, marked `(external)`, so pointing at `entire agent list --external` sent the user to repeat a search whose results were four lines above.
    - A targeted single-name lookup ran → `externalAgentSearchedHint(name)`, which names the one plugin that came up missing. This is `agent add` / `agent remove`.
    - No lookup at all → `externalAgentHint`, now down to exactly one caller: the `--agent` `FlagErrorFunc`, which cobra invokes during flag parsing, before `enable`'s `RunE` and so before its scan.
    - `printMissingAgentError` was reached from both sides of that line, so it splits into `…PreDiscovery` / `…PostDiscovery`. `printAgentError` treats an empty hint as omit, with no stray blank line left behind.
  - The usage line follows the caller's command surface (`entire agent add` / `entire agent remove` / `entire enable --agent`) instead of always printing `entire enable --agent`.
- **New `agent.ListAvailable() []ResolvedAgent`** is the single place the test-only filter lives; `StringList`, `runAgentList`, `printAgentError`, and `hookAgentOptions` (the interactive agent picker, which carried its own inline `TestOnly` check) all go through it, so "which agents are available" has one answer across the command surface. No inline test-only checks remain outside `registry.go`. It returns name+agent pairs because an external plugin's self-reported `Name()` is not validated against the registry key derived from its binary, and the registry key is the identity users type and `agent.Get` accepts.
  - `agent.Get`'s unknown-agent error was the last unfiltered user-facing listing — `main.go` prints it verbatim where a command doesn't intercept it, and it named `vogon`. It now lists `StringList()`, with the read lock released before the message is formatted so `StringList` (which resolves each agent through `Get`) can't re-enter `registryMu`. That also removes the latent nested `RLock` the old `List()` call had on that line.
  - The pre-existing `List` and `StringList` keep their names. `List` stays deliberately unfiltered because the registry's own plumbing needs every registered name: `hooks_cmd.go` builds the `entire hooks <agent> <verb>` subcommands from it and the Vogon binary invokes `entire hooks vogon <verb>`, so filtering there would break every canary test; `external/discovery.go` needs the full set to avoid re-registering a name already taken. Renaming these for clarity is a separate concern and stays out of this PR.
- **New `agent.IsRegistered`** for existence probes. `external/discovery.go` was asking "is this name taken?" by discarding a `Get` error, which built the whole `available: ...` listing (resolving every registered agent) just to answer yes/no.
- `agent.SnapshotForTesting` moved to `cmd/entire/cli/agent/testing.go` — it cannot live in a `_test.go` because package `cli`'s tests need it, and the filename follows `internal/entireclient/tokenstore/testing.go`, the existing precedent for a dedicated cross-package test-helper file. Its doc comment is narrowed: capture/restore are safe against concurrent registry *readers*, not writers, since restore replaces the whole map.
- Docs: `docs/architecture/external-agent-protocol.md` claimed discovery "runs once during CLI initialization". There is no such step — every call site is inside a command, in one of three shapes (gated full scan, ungated full scan, ungated single-name lookup). The Discovery section now documents which commands use which, that `external_agents` gates the first, and how `agent list` and `--external` differ. `CLAUDE.md`'s command-layout entry for `agent` gained the same `list` / `list --external` / `add`-`remove` distinction.
- Drive-by, unrelated to external agents: `agent/architecture_test.go` had `//nolint:staticcheck` separated from the `parser.ParseDir` call by another comment line, where the directive does not apply. Moved onto the offending line.

## Test
- `TestRunAgentList_ExternalFlagListsAvailablePlugin`: the default listing does not surface an available external plugin; `--external` lists it.
- `TestRunAgentList_DefaultPathDoesNotScanPath`: asserts on an exec log the mock plugin appends to, proving the default path never execs a plugin while `--external` does — the guarantee the filter-driven absence check above cannot make.
- `TestRunAgentList_ExternalFlagMarksInstalled`: `--external` lists an installed external plugin marked `✓`.
- `TestRunAgentList_ExternalIsSuperset`: `--external` includes both the external plugin and the built-ins.
- `TestRunAgentList_MarksExternalProvenance`: external lines carry `(external)`, built-in lines do not.
- `TestRunAgentList_HeaderScopedToMode`: the default header scopes itself to built-ins; `--external`, the complete view, does not.
- `TestRunAgentList_DefaultFooterNamesEnabledGate`: with `external_agents` on, the default listing reports the plugins it is omitting; with the gate unset it prints the plain `--external` pointer and does not claim the gate is on.
- `TestRunAgentList_EmptyStateWording`: mode-scoped empty state — "No built-in agents installed" by default, "No agents installed" under `--external`.
- `TestEnableCmd_UnknownAgent_ListsPluginsAndOmitsHint` executes the real `enable` `RunE` with a mock plugin on `$PATH` and asserts the plugin appears marked `(external)` **and** that no hint follows. This is the test that had to exist: the pre-existing unit test passed only because it called `printWrongAgentError` directly with the hint hardcoded, never triggering the discovery that made the hint wrong. Verified red by reverting just the `enable` call site.
- `TestPrintAgentError_ExcludesTestOnlyAgents`, `TestPrintAgentError_PointsAtExternalListing`, `TestPrintAgentError_HintReflectsWhatWasSearched` (inverted: after a full scan, neither hint wording may appear, and no doubled blank line), `TestAgentAdd_UnknownNameReportsSearchedPath`, and the usage-line assertion in `TestPrintWrongAgentError` cover the error-path fixes.
- `TestSnapshotForTesting_RestoresRegistry` covers the registry snapshot helper; `TestIsRegistered` pins that the probe answers for test-only agents too, since it reports registry membership rather than user-facing availability.
- `TestGet_UnknownAgentErrorExcludesTestOnly` pins that `Get`'s error lists real agents and not test-only ones (verified red before green; the package also passes under `-race`, since the fix changes locking).
- The external-plugin tests share one `withExternalAgentPlugin` helper (isolated repo, `#!/bin/sh` mock plugin on a scrubbed `$PATH`, registry snapshot/restore), parameterised on the two axes that actually differ: whether the mock reports its hooks installed, and whether the settings enable `external_agents` — the listing tests opt in, `add`/`remove` deliberately leave it unset because naming a plugin is itself the opt-in. They skip when no POSIX shell is available.

## Verification
- `mise run fmt` — clean
- `mise run lint` (golangci-lint 2.11.3) — 0 issues
- `mise run test:ci` — PASS
- Benchmark (9 shell plugins on `$PATH`, `external_agents:true`): default `agent list` **18 execs → 0**; external listing moved behind `--external`. Wall clock for the opt-in path, min of 6 runs: default 1.13s vs `--external` 1.69s, i.e. ~60ms per plugin for the two subcommands discovery invokes.

This is the test that had to exist: the pre-existing unit test passed only because it called `printWrongAgentError` directly with the hint hardcoded, never triggering the discovery that made the hint wrong. Verified red by reverting just the `enable` call site.
- `TestPrintAgentError_ExcludesTestOnlyAgents`, `TestPrintAgentError_PointsAtExternalListing`, `TestPrintAgentError_HintReflectsWhatWasSearched` (inverted: after a full scan, neither hint wording may appear, and no doubled blank line), `TestAgentAdd_UnknownNameReportsSearchedPath`, and the usage-line assertion in `TestPrintWrongAgentError` cover the error-path fixes.
- `TestSnapshotForTesting_RestoresRegistry` covers the registry snapshot helper; `TestIsRegistered` pins that the probe answers for test-only agents too, since it reports registry membership rather than user-facing availability.
- `TestGet_UnknownAgentErrorExcludesTestOnly` pins that `Get`'s error lists real agents and not test-only ones (verified red before green; the package also passes under `-race`, since the fix changes locking).
- The external-plugin tests share one `withExternalAgentPlugin` helper (isolated repo, `#!/bin/sh` mock plugin on a scrubbed `$PATH`, registry snapshot/restore), parameterised on the two axes that actually differ: whether the mock reports its hooks installed, and whether the settings enable `external_agents` — the listing tests opt in, `add`/`remove` deliberately leave it unset because naming a plugin is itself the opt-in. They skip when no POSIX shell is available.

- `mise run fmt` — clean
- `mise run lint` (golangci-lint 2.11.3) — 0 issues
- `mise run test:ci` — PASS

Add the smallest test that fails for the reproduced bug and would pass once the
bug is fixed.

## Do

- Put the test next to the closest existing coverage.
- Use real inputs and observable outputs.
- Name the test after the broken behavior, not the implementation detail.
- Run only the focused test first and confirm it fails for the expected reason.
- Do not duplicate production logic inside the test.

- Test file and test name.
- Focused command used to run it.
- Failure output proving the test catches the bug.

manual verification command or script instead.

wait i am asking you to explain the bug to me

No commit was made. Let’s pause and unpack the bug properly.

The core idea is that Entire has two settings scopes:

```text
.entire/settings.json        shared project settings, usually committed
.entire/settings.local.json  personal settings, usually uncommitted
```

When Entire runs, it merges them:

```text
project settings
      +
local overrides
      =
effective runtime settings
```

That merge is correct for reading. The bug was using that merged result for writing.

## Concrete example

Suppose the project file contains:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "push": false
  }
}
```

Your personal local file contains:

```json
{
  "log_level": "debug"
}
```

At runtime, Entire needs both, so `LoadEntireSettings()` produces approximately:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "strategy_options": {
    "push": false
  },
  "log_level": "debug"
}
```

Now you add an external agent and choose to save that choice to the project settings.

The only intended change is:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "push": false
  },
  "external_agents": true
}
```

But the old code did this conceptually:

```go
settings := LoadEntireSettings() // merged project + local settings
settings.ExternalAgents = true
SaveProjectSettings(settings)    // writes the entire merged object
```

Therefore, the project file became:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "log_level": "debug",
  "strategy_options": {
    "push": false
  },
  "external_agents": true
}
```

Your personal `log_level` crossed into the shared project file. That is the “scope leak.”

The reverse also happened: when targeting local settings, project-only values could be copied into the local file.

## Why this matters

It is more than untidy JSON.

- Personal paths or logging preferences could accidentally be committed.
- Local checkpoint-remote choices could become project-wide configuration.
- Project values copied into the local file could later shadow legitimate project changes.
- Default values such as `"enabled": true` could appear even though the user only changed `external_agents`.
- Once the settings are merged, the program no longer knows which file each value originally came from.

A good analogy is editing CSS from computed styles. The browser may calculate a final style from five stylesheets, but you cannot safely write that computed result back into one stylesheet—the result has lost its provenance.

## What we changed

The new behavior is conceptually:

```go
target := chooseProjectOrLocalFile()
settings := loadRawJSON(target)
settings["external_agents"] = true
saveRawJSON(target, settings)
```

So we:

1. Resolve the specific file the user selected.
2. Read only that file—not the merged runtime view.
3. Change only `external_agents`.
4. Write the same file back.

We use raw JSON instead of loading the typed settings structure because that also preserves fields this CLI version might not recognize. A typed round trip could inject defaults or discard newer fields.

## How we proved it was real

The regression test exercises the interactive agent-management path in both directions:

```text
local log_level → project target
project log_level → local target
```

Before the fix, both cases failed:

```text
log_level from the opposite settings scope leaked into .entire/settings.json
log_level from the opposite settings scope leaked into .entire/settings.local.json
```

After the fix, both pass. The test also checks that:

- the target’s pre-existing `strategy_options` remains;
- `external_agents` becomes `true`;
- no additional fields appear.

One subtle detail: the non-interactive setup path had already been fixed to use scoped settings. The defect survived specifically in the interactive agent-management path.

Quick understanding check: if project settings say `"log_level":"warn"` and local settings say `"log_level":"debug"`, which value should runtime code read—and which value should remain in the project file when only `external_agents` is changed?

```json
    "push": false
  }
}
```

Your personal local file contains:

```json
{
  "log_level": "debug"
}
```

At runtime, Entire needs both, so `LoadEntireSettings()` produces approximately:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "strategy_options": {
    "push": false
  },
  "log_level": "debug"
}
```

Now you add an external agent and choose to save that choice to the project settings.

The only intended change is:

```json
{
  "strategy_options": {
    "push": false
  },
  "external_agents": true
}
```

But the old code did this conceptually:

```go
settings := LoadEntireSettings() // merged project + local settings
settings.ExternalAgents = true
SaveProjectSettings(settings)    // writes the entire merged object
```

Therefore, the project file became:

```json
{
  "enabled": true,
  "log_level": "debug",
  "strategy_options": {
    "push": false
  },
  "external_agents": true
}
```

Your personal `log_level` crossed into the shared project file. That is the “scope leak.”

The reverse also happened: when targeting local settings, project-only values could be copied into the local file.

## Why this matters

It is more than untidy JSON.

- Personal paths or logging preferences could accidentally be committed.
- Local checkpoint-remote choices could become project-wide configuration.
- Project values copied into the local file could later shadow legitimate project changes.
- Default values such as `"enabled": true` could appear even though the user only changed `external_agents`.
- Once the settings are merged, the program no longer knows which file each value originally came from.

A good analogy is editing CSS from computed styles. The browser may calculate a final style from five stylesheets, but you cannot safely write that computed result back into one stylesheet—the result has lost its provenance.

## What we changed

The new behavior is conceptually:

```go
target := chooseProjectOrLocalFile()
settings := loadRawJSON(target)
settings["external_agents"] = true
saveRawJSON(target, settings)
```

So we:

1. Resolve the specific file the user selected.
2. Read only that file—not the merged runtime view.
3. Change only `external_agents`.
4. Write the same file back.

We use raw JSON instead of loading the typed settings structure because that also preserves fields this CLI version might not recognize. A typed round trip could inject defaults or discard newer fields.

## How we proved it was real

The regression test exercises the interactive agent-management path in both directions:

```text
local log_level → project target
project log_level → local target
```

Before the fix, both cases failed:

```text
log_level from the opposite settings scope leaked into .entire/settings.json
log_level from the opposite settings scope leaked into .entire/settings.local.json
```

After the fix, both pass. The test also checks that:

- the target’s pre-existing `strategy_options` remains;
- `external_agents` becomes `true`;
- no additional fields appear.

One subtle detail: the non-interactive setup path had already been fixed to use scoped settings. The defect survived specifically in the interactive agent-management path.

Quick understanding check: if project settings say `"log_level":"warn"` and local settings say `"log_level":"debug"`, which value should runtime code read—and which value should remain in the project file when only `external_agents` is changed?

content.text: no but how is this a bug?
no but how is this a bug?

Because the command changes settings the user did not ask it to change—and those changes affect other people or future behavior.

The merge itself is not the bug. Persisting the merged result into one scope is.

Consider this timeline:

1. The committed project settings contain no log-level preference.
2. You personally use this local override:

```json
{ "log_level": "debug" }
```

3. You run “add external agent” and select the project scope.
4. You expect one project change:

```json
{ "external_agents": true }
```

5. Instead, the command also writes your personal preference into the committed file:

```json
{
  "external_agents": true,
  "log_level": "debug"
}
```

6. You commit that file. Now every teammate gets debug logging, even though nobody intentionally chose that project-wide setting.

That is observable incorrect behavior: an operation on `external_agents` silently changes an unrelated setting’s ownership from “personal” to “shared.”

The reverse direction creates another real failure:

1. Project settings specify a checkpoint remote.
2. Adding an external agent locally copies that remote into your local file.
3. Later, the project changes its checkpoint remote.
4. Your accidentally copied local value continues overriding the new project value.
5. Your machine uses the stale remote, even though you never configured a personal override.

So the bug violates three expectations:

- Scope: `--project` and `--local` identify which configuration layer is being changed.
- Minimality: adding an agent should change `external_agents`, not unrelated settings.
- Precedence: a temporary copied value can become a permanent override and change future behavior.

In one sentence: **the command accidentally converts inherited settings into explicitly owned settings.** That changes who receives them and how future configuration updates behave.
